Journey · Children’s Books

Answers (p. 76–80)

Pages 76–80 (5 pages)
Page 76

Answers Quiz 1 (chapters 1 and 2) 1. (b) no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air. “Right understanding can be developed no matter where one is, on land, on water or in the air.” The travellers talked about the Dhamma by the pyramids, on a boat and on the plane. 2. (b) a conditioned reality that can be experienced at this moment. “The phenomena that occur at this moment and that can be experienced through the senses and the mind can be called “dhammas”, conditioned realities.” With a capital letter, the Dhamma (the teaching) is “the Buddha’s teaching of all that is real”. 3. Eyesense and visible object. “Nobody can cause the arising of seeing, seeing has its own conditions for its arising. Without eyesense and visible object it could not arise.” 4. False. “Only one citta arises at a time and it is accompanied by several mental factors, cetasikas.” Seeing and hearing never happen in the same moment, however quickly they follow one another. 5. (b) the sound of the bell. Sound experiences nothing: “Physical phenomena or rūpa do not experience any object.” Hearing, liking and remembering all experience something, so they are nāma (mind). 6. “the Vinaya or Book of Discipline for the monks, the Suttanta or Discourses and the Abhidhamma which is an exposition of all realities in detail.” 7. (b) The Abhidhamma is not in the book. ““The Abhidhamma is not in the book”, as Acharn said.” Nina explains: “The Abhidhamma deals with whatever is experienced in daily life; it deals with what is pleasant or unpleasant, wholesome or unwholesome.” 8. (b) conventional truth, the world of concepts. “Conventional truth is the world of concepts such as person, tree or animal we can think of but which are not real in the ultimate sense. Ultimate realities, nāma and rūpa, are impermanent, they arise and fall away.” 9. “when we remember that unpleasant experiences through the senses are vipākacittas conditioned by our own kamma, not by another person, we shall be less inclined to blame others.” What is heard is the result of one’s own past kamma (deed). 10. 1. listening to the Dhamma; 2. intellectual understanding of what the Buddha taught; 3. direct understanding of the realities that appear. “Because of listening to the Dhamma, we acquire intellectual understanding of what the Buddha taught and then we gradually learn to verify in our life the truth of the phenomena that occur so that there can be direct understanding.” 11. True. Acharn “would emphasize that we should not think of ourselves, and that we become less selfish by paying more attention to the needs of others.” Nina calls it “a simple advice, but it is very basic.” 12. (b) ignorance, attachment and aversion. “Akusala cetasikas such as ignorance, attachment and aversion accompany akusala citta. Wholesome cetasikas such as kindness or understanding accompany kusala citta.” Quiz 2 (chapters 3 and 4) 1. (b) patience. “patience is mentioned first, and this is very appropriate.” In the Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching) the same teaching is given, but the order is different. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 76

Page 77

2. “Without patience one cannot attain enlightenment”. Nina adds: “We need great patience to develop understanding of all realities of our daily life.” 3. False. “Patience should be developed not only when the object is unpleasant but also when it is pleasant. When a pleasant object presents itself, usually lobha arises and in that case there is no patience.” 4. (b) impatience. “at the moment of akusala citta there is impatience and at the moment of kusala citta there is patience.” Patience is not something a person owns; it is there whenever the citta (consciousness) is kusala (wholesome). 5. “Awareness is non-forgetfulness of what is wholesome, kusala.” Awareness of the level of satipaṭṭhāna (direct awareness of realities) “is directly aware of mental phenomena, nāma, and physical phenomena, rūpa, as they appear one at a time through one of the six doors.” 6. (b) she understood the ugliness of aversion and said nothing about the crying. “When someone’s baby was crying she understood the ugliness of aversion and that was a condition for kusala citta: she would not say anything about the baby’s crying.” Acharn said: “This shows progress in the development of right understanding”. 7. (b) Do you like it to be tired?. “Acharn asked him, “Do you like it to be tired?” Alan answered that he did not like it and then it became clear that he had aversion.” 8. False. “We use tiredness as an excuse not to develop kusala at such a moment but, Acharn said, it is no excuse.” 9. “When the luggage did not come I was so impatient, I lifted my hands. That was conditioned by impatience. There was no awareness.” 10. (a) if you do not understand the disadvantage of akusala you will have more akusala.. “Nothing can hinder paññā. However, if you do not understand the disadvantage of akusala you will have more akusala. People desire great paññā, but is there paññā that sees the uselessness of akusala at this moment?” 11. “Do not think of it, let it go. Everything just arises because of conditions. It is of no use to try to control your body. Awareness is aware naturally, this is the way. Develop understanding at any time, also when you cannot control your stomach.” Alan came along on the plane and was not sick any more. 12. (b) It is my time to help. “You can think: ‘It is my time to help’, and then kusala citta can arise. Everything can be changed by right understanding.” Quiz 3 (chapters 5 and 6) 1. (b) it remembers what is seen, and cittas think of it for a long time. “The cetasika saññā, remembrance or perception, remembers what is seen and cittas think of it for a long time.” The seeing lasts a moment; the thinking about it lasts much longer. 2. “It is only a story in your mind. Previous experiences condition the thought of a being.” What is seen is colour; “there is nobody in the visible object.” 3. (b) Now you are preparing.. “When I said that we have to be prepared, she said: “Now you are preparing.”” Nina writes: “We can only prepare ourselves for a great loss by understanding the present moment more clearly.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 77

Page 78

4. False. “You do not have to try to prevent thinking. When thinking thinks a great deal, it is time to understand thinking.” 5. (b) the darkness in between the acts, when the curtain is drawn. “The cittas experiencing the sense objects are the actors and the bhavanga-cittas in between processes are like the darkness in between the acts, when the curtain is drawn.” 6. “Praise is called an axe that falls from heaven. It wounds if one does not know how to receive it.” Acharn said: “We should learn to receive both blame and praise.” 7. “generosity, morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, lovingkindness and equanimity.” 8. (b) to extend mettā to different people at any time, and not to particular people. “My goal is not infinite mettā, but to extend mettā to different people at any time, and not to particular people.” 9. True. Nina writes: “It should not disturb us that we cannot attain enlightenment soon, that it takes aeons. Gabi said: ”Thinking of aeons will make patience grow.”” 10. (c) Alan. Alan said: “My family and friends are not interested at all, so one has to go against the stream. It takes quite an effort to turn away from what most people follow and to go your own way.” 11. A lay disciple at the Buddha’s time. “At the age of seven she became a sotāpanna, after she heard the Buddha preach. Later on she married and she had ten sons and ten daughters.” She was “foremost in ministering to the Sangha”. “She understood her clinging as a conditioned reality, not self.” 12. (b) because there is no surer foundation than truthful speech, and one who forsakes the truth cannot attain Buddhahood. “in this world there is no surer foundation than truthful speech. Someone who forsakes the truth cannot attain Buddhahood, even if he sits in the sacred enclosure of the Bodhi Tree. Hence I should only speak the truth.” Quiz 4 (chapters 7 and 8) 1. (b) Why do you want it? Develop it.. “Why do you want it? Develop it.” Nina calls this “a short but pointed reminder; it helped us to know our clinging to understanding.” 2. False. “We want to be “somebody with sati”, but it is more beneficial to remember that we are “nobody”. That is in accordance with the truth. There is no self who could plan to have sati.” 3. “If you don’t wish but you develop it, it is more beneficial.” And when Nina said she could not help wishing: “If you understand that wishing is of no use, there is a condition for awareness.” 4. (a) a person.. “The Buddha taught ultimate realities, paramaṭṭha dhammas, so that one can understand the meaning of no being, no person, no self. It is citta which knows an object, not a person.” 5. (b) you can’t prevent it from arising. “When there are conditions for awareness, you can’t prevent it from arising”. Nina explains: “When the conditions are right it must arise and we do not have to do anything to cause its arising.” 6. False. Buddhaghosa classified the levels of each; “There is no rule with regard to a specific order of the development of the different types of kusala.” 7. “One level of paññā is seeing the disadvantage of akusala, another level of paññā is studying and considering the Dhamma, and another level again is paññā developed in satipaṭṭhāna.” 8. (b) a bud which will appear on a tree. “Paññā is like a bud which will appear on a tree. One does not know where and when it will appear. We should not care when it will appear; what about the A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 78

Page 79

understanding of this moment?” 9. (b) looking at a painting. “When we look at somebody it is exactly the same as looking at a painting, Acharn said.” What is seen is colour; the person is thought of afterwards. 10. “Nobody can change the conditions for each different colour. You cannot change the colour of Gabi’s eyes. Colour is just a kind of rūpa which can be seen through the eyes.” Colours do not have to be named; they appear because of conditions, and nobody can change them. 11. (b) I always follow the stream. “She said: “I always follow the stream”.” Nina writes: “When we try to change events we are bound to have aversion and we have no patience.” 12. “Evenso one should guard oneself; let not a moment slip.” Nina writes: “We should “guard ourselves”, but without any idea of “self”.” The guard is sati (awareness), not a person. Quiz 5 (chapters 9 and 10) 1. (b) on a boat on the Bosporus. “Acharn Sujin explained about Buddhism to our guide in Turkey, Ms. Tuna, while we were having a tour on the Bosporus river.” 2. “When one is sleeping where is the soul?” Ms Tuna did not know. Acharn went on to ask whether it is the soul which sees and the soul which hears. 3. (b) seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching and thinking. “Seeing is one function, hearing is another function. Besides these, there are the functions of smelling, tasting, touching and thinking. I believe that the soul sleeps too.” 4. (b) consciousness, because soul implies something permanent. “We can use the word consciousness instead of soul. The word soul can give rise to misunderstandings, it is not precise enough. If we use the word soul it implies something permanent. Consciousness experiences one object at a time and it is not permanent; it changes all the time.” 5. False. “Seeing is seeing for everyone, it does not belong to any race or nationality. Also animals see. Seeing is the same no matter what you call it.” 6. Cooking. “In order to be a good person you have to develop wholesomeness, you have to train yourself. Just as when you want to be skillful in cooking you have to train yourself so that one day you will be a good cook.” 7. (b) attachment, aversion and ignorance. “Three basic defilements are roots for unwholesome states of mind, namely: attachment, anger or aversion, and ignorance.” In Pali: lobha (attachment), dosa (aversion), moha (ignorance). 8. False. “Anger is always unwholesome, no matter what the cause is. It harms yourself and others. This does not mean that you cannot be firm with others when it is necessary for people’s benefit, but hatred and anger are always unwholesome.” 9. “Unselfish love is characterised by considering the welfare of others. Attachment to other people is for the sake of one’s own pleasant feeling.” 10. (b) pleasure; understanding. “We can enjoy all the pleasant things but we should at the same time develop more understanding of the realities of our life. … A wise person can live with pleasure and with understanding.” 11. (b) hardness. “In reality, it is hardness which is experienced through the bodysense, not a cup, plate or chair. When hardness is experienced we know through memory that there is a cup, plate or chair”. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 79

Page 80

12. “Through bodysense the realities of hardness, softness, heat, cold, motion or pressure can be experienced. They are true for everybody, no matter how we name them.” 13. True. “Right understanding can eliminate ignorance and wrong view. Through right understanding there will be less clinging, and that means more freedom.” Quiz 6 (chapters 11 and 12) 1. (b) meditation. “I avoid using the word meditation because different people have different ideas about it. Our goal should be the development of right understanding of the realities which appear now.” 2. False. “Not at all, because the purpose of the Buddha’s teachings is to understand the realities which arise naturally, in daily life.” “Sound is a reality, no matter where you are, whether it is quiet or whether there is a lot of noise.” 3. “When it does not appear there is still the latent tendency of wrong view. This is like a virus which is latent in the body but which can become active at any time.” 4. (b) every moment, whether you work or you don’t work. “You can start again at every moment, whether you work or you don’t work, whether you are in a hurry or at leisure, it is the same. You always have an opportunity to start again.” 5. (b) the eyes, the ears, the nose, the tongue, the body and the mind. Realities “appear only one at a time through one of the six doorways”: the five senses and the mind-door. 6. “No. We should understand thinking as thinking, seeing as seeing, feeling as feeling; they are different realities.” 7. False. “There is no predestined fate ruling over our life. However, the different moments of our life are conditioned by the past and by the present.” 8. (b) when one is no longer interested in developing understanding. “When one is no longer interested in developing understanding.” And: “Even if it is difficult to develop understanding there are so many moments for you to start again.” 9. (b) It is just this moment.. “Sometimes she was yawning and when I asked her whether she was tired she answered: ”It is just this moment.”” 10. “I am most grateful to Acharn for pointing out to us time and again that we should understand our life at this very moment. What she explained is completely in conformity with the Buddha’s teachings.” 11. (b) all the moments of studying and considering the Dhamma and all the other kinds of kusala. “All the moments of studying and considering the Dhamma and all the other kinds of kusala are never lost, they are accumulated from one moment to the next moment so that they can arise again, later on.” 12. “The Abhidhamma deals with whatever is experienced in daily life; it deals with what is pleasant or unpleasant, wholesome or unwholesome.” 13. (b) to people who thought they could not attain enlightenment in this life and gave up. “Some people become discouraged when they think that they cannot attain enlightenment in this life, and then they give up the development of satipaṭṭhāna. … The understanding of this moment leads to the goal. “Develop it now, be aware now”, Acharn often said.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 80
